title: Testing the app the way users use it

steps.headline: Each release must prove the finished app works for a real user, on every platform, before it ships.
steps.changed: Today about 6,300 automatic tests check small parts of the app on their own. Not one starts the finished app, which is how 1.3.1–1.3.3 shipped a phone app that can't start its assistant and nobody noticed the games server vanished.
steps.notice: Before every release, a short report lists the things a real user does — open the app, chat, sync, play a game — and says each one was tried on the real downloadable build and worked.

steps.headline: No test ever checks exact wording or styling again; the ones that do are deleted or loosened.
steps.changed: About 1 in 8 tests (maybe 1 in 5) freeze wording, a style name or how the code is laid out, and break on harmless changes. Another 1 in 8 that check real behaviour also check exact wording on the side.
steps.notice: Rewording a button or restyling a screen stops causing failed tests and busywork. Wording and looks are checked by you, by eye, on the visual change review below.

steps.headline: Tests for your personal Home Assistant and money pages move out of the app's test suite.
steps.changed: 5 of the 150 tests sampled cover pages that live only on your computer and never ship in the app, yet run on every app change.
steps.notice: App checks get slightly faster. Your personal pages keep their tests, in their own folder, so they still catch breaks there.

steps.page: What the real-app check walks through
steps.intro: These are the things the check does on the real app, the way a new user would. Tick everything that must work before a release can ship.

steps.headline: Which of these must the real-app check try before every release?
steps.today: None of these is tried on a real build before release. Your Android test on 2026-11-01 found show-stoppers in the first hour.
steps.problem: Each one left untried is a way a release can ship broken without anyone knowing until users hit it.
steps.proposal: Pick every one that must work. Each says what it would have caught and what it costs to check. More picks = a longer check, not a harder one.

options.label: Download, install, open
options.summary: Install the real release file on a clean machine or phone, open it, and see the first screen.
pros: Catches an app that won't open or shows a blank window.
Catches a first screen that spills off a phone (found 2026-11-01).
cons: Needs clean test machines for each platform; those exist for Windows, Mac and Linux.

options.label: Sign in and first chat
options.summary: As a brand-new user: sign in, start a chat with Claude Code and with the app's own assistant, and get a reply.
pros: Would have caught 'can't start its assistant' — the 1.3.1–1.3.3 phone failure.
Would have caught the hidden Claude Code setup screen that blocks a new user's first chat.
cons: Each run uses a little real assistant usage (see cost question).

options.label: Real chat tasks
options.summary: A set of ordinary requests that use many tools: write and save a file, research online, run a command, build a Page, a long task with the app in the background.
pros: Proves the assistant can actually do work, not just reply.
Catches broken tools and permission cards that don't show.
cons: The slowest part — a few minutes per task.
Answers vary run to run, so it checks the outcome (file saved, Page made) rather than exact words.

options.label: Make, open, edit, save files
options.summary: Open a saved file in the viewer, edit it (text, Word, spreadsheet), save, and reopen it to check nothing was lost.
pros: Catches lost edits and files that won't open.
Catches 'attach file does nothing' (found 2026-11-01).
cons: Office files need extra setup on each test machine.

options.label: Manage sessions
options.summary: Rename a chat, add tags and notes, resume it after closing the app, search old chats.
pros: Catches lost names, tags or notes after a restart.
Catches Resume not finding old chats.
cons: Fast and cheap; nothing big against it.

options.label: Backup & sync
options.summary: Turn on sync, change something on one device, and see it arrive on another.
pros: Would have caught 'sync always fails on Android' (found 2026-11-01).
cons: Needs a test sync account and two devices or two test copies.
Slower: waits for the round trip.

options.label: Games
options.summary: Play a solo game, and connect two test players for an online game.
pros: Would have caught the online games server vanishing (found 2026-11-01).
Catches 2048 not working with swipes on a phone.
cons: Two test players means two app copies running at once.

options.label: Assistant's browser
options.summary: Ask the assistant to open a website, read it and click something.
pros: Catches the browser panel failing to open or the assistant losing control of it.
cons: Depends on a website staying up; we'd use a page we control.

options.label: Install a skill and theme
options.summary: Browse the marketplace, install a skill and a theme, apply the theme, use the skill.
pros: Catches a broken marketplace or an install that silently fails.
cons: Leaves a test install behind on the test machine (cleaned up after).

options.label: Phone connects to computer
options.summary: Connect the phone app to a computer running the app and chat through it.
pros: Catches the phone hiding its 'connect to computer' screen (found 2026-11-01).
cons: Needs a phone and a computer on the same network during the check.

steps.headline: Is anything a user does missing from that list?
steps.today: The list above came from your 2026-11-01 Android test and your message: games, sync, sessions, browser, files, chat tasks.
steps.problem: Anything left off won't be tried before a release.
steps.proposal: Type anything missing, or leave it at Don't know.
steps.prompt: e.g. voice input, buddy, remote access from a browser…

steps.intro: These decide how close to a real user the check gets, and what it costs.

steps.headline: How should the check be split between every code change and every release?
steps.today: Every code change runs about 6,300 small tests in the cloud (free, ~minutes). Releases add one check that the computer app's window isn't blank.
steps.problem: Running the full user walk-through on every change would be slow; running it only at release means a break can sit unnoticed for weeks before release day.
steps.proposal: Two layers: a quick 'does the real app start and answer one message' on every change, and the full walk-through on real installed builds before each release.

options.label: Quick check + full walk-through
options.summary: Every change: start the real app engine on Linux and phone-style hardware in the cloud, send one message. Every release: the full list above on real installed builds.
pros: A startup crash like the phone's is caught the same day it's written, not at release.
The full walk-through still happens before anything ships.
Cloud machines are free for an open-source project like YouCoded.
cons: Two things to build instead of one.
The quick check adds a few minutes to every change.

options.label: Full walk-through at release only
pros: One thing to build.
No extra wait on everyday changes.
cons: A break can sit unnoticed for weeks and pile up with others before release day, making it harder to find what caused it.

options.label: Full walk-through every change
pros: Every break found almost immediately.
cons: Probably 30–60 minutes per change (rough guess).
Uses real assistant usage dozens of times a day.

steps.headline: Who judges the walk-through: a script with pass/fail rules, an AI tester using the app like a person, or both?
steps.today: Your 2026-11-01 Android test was an AI session using the app like a person. It found the 6 show-stoppers and 23 smaller problems, like the welcome card spilling off the screen and 'computer' wording on a phone.
steps.problem: A script only catches what it was told to look for ('was the file saved?'). It misses 'this feels broken' — confusing wording, things off screen, a button that should exist.
steps.proposal: A script decides pass/fail for the must-work list, and an AI tester then explores like a new user and writes up anything that felt wrong.

options.label: Both
pros: The script gives a clear yes/no that can stop a release.
The AI tester catches the 'this feels wrong' problems a script never would — most of what your Android test found.
cons: The AI tester's report needs a read each release (a few minutes).
It can report things that are fine; you'd skim and dismiss those.

options.label: Script only
pros: Same result every time; nothing to read.
cons: Misses layout, wording and 'feels broken' problems.

options.label: AI tester only
pros: Closest to a real user; one thing to build.
cons: No firm yes/no to stop a release; results vary run to run.

steps.headline: Should the check's chats use the real assistant, or pre-recorded replies?
steps.today: Nothing in testing talks to a real assistant today.
steps.problem: Pre-recorded replies are free but can't notice that a real sign-in or a real model stopped working — like the outside games server, the thing you depend on can vanish.
steps.proposal: Real assistant for the release walk-through, with a spending cap; pre-recorded replies for the quick everyday check.

options.label: Real at release, recorded daily
pros: The release proves real sign-in and real replies work.
Everyday checks cost nothing.
cons: Roughly $1–3 of model usage per release walk-through, plus some of your Claude plan's usage (rough guess; I'd measure the first run).

options.label: Real assistant always
pros: Most realistic everywhere.
cons: Cost grows with every code change, maybe dozens of runs a day.

options.label: Recorded replies always
pros: Free.
cons: Can't catch a broken sign-in or a model that stopped working.

steps.headline: What phone should the release check run on?
steps.today: The only Android test so far ran on your Flip7 over a cable, with side-by-side test copies. The emulator on the computer can't run the app's bundled programs.
steps.problem: A phone check that needs you there each release will get skipped on busy days — that's partly how 1.3.1–1.3.3 shipped untried.
steps.proposal: A cheap dedicated Android phone, always plugged into this computer, so the phone check runs by itself.

options.label: A cheap test phone
pros: Runs without you; never touches your own phone.
Can be wiped clean before each run, like a new user's phone.
cons: About $150–250 once.
Stays plugged into this computer.

options.label: Your Flip7
pros: Free; already proven to work.
cons: Needs you to plug it in and leave it unlocked ~20–40 minutes each release.
Easy to skip when busy.

options.label: Rented cloud phones
pros: Many phone models; nothing to plug in.
cons: Pay per minute each run.
Harder to set up for sign-in and two-device tests like sync.

steps.headline: Should a daily check confirm the outside services the app relies on still exist?
steps.today: The games server, marketplace, sign-in pages and model providers are outside the app. When the games server vanished, nothing noticed.
steps.problem: These can break any day, with no code change from us, so a release check alone would miss them for weeks.
steps.proposal: Yes: a free daily check visits each one and alerts you (e.g. a work board card) if one stops answering. No: rely on the release check and user reports.

steps.headline: If the release check fails, should the release be stopped?
steps.today: Releases go out after code-reading reviews and the small tests pass. No check of the real app can stop one.
steps.problem: A check that only warns tends to get waved through on release day.

options.label: Stop, unless you say why
pros: Nothing ships broken by accident.
You can still ship deliberately — e.g. a fix for something worse — with your reason written into the release record.
cons: A false alarm in the check delays the release until it's looked at.

options.label: Always stop
pros: Strictest.
cons: A broken test machine could hold up an urgent fix.

options.label: Warn only
pros: Never delays a release.
cons: Easy to ignore, which is the situation today.

steps.intro: This replaces the wording and styling tests: you look instead.

steps.headline: Should the work board get a 'What changed since last release' button?
steps.today: The Screens tab shows a picture of every screen at one point in time. The screenshot tool can compare two versions, but only when a session runs it for one piece of work.
steps.problem: There's no one place to see every look and wording change heading into a release, so surprises reach users.
steps.proposal: One button photographs every screen on the last release and on the latest code, and lists only the screens that changed, with the changed parts highlighted.

options.label: Changed screens, highlighted
pros: You see only what's different, so it stays short.
Highlights point at the exact change, including one-word wording edits.
cons: Photographing every screen twice takes a while (likely 10–20 minutes; it can run ahead of time).

options.label: Every screen, side by side
pros: Nothing filtered out.
cons: Hundreds of identical pairs to scroll past.

steps.headline: Should approving those changed screens be part of every release?
steps.today: Nothing asks you to look at a release's screens before it ships.
steps.problem: Without a step, the review is easy to skip.
steps.proposal: Yes: each changed screen gets Keep / Not this, and the release waits until every one is answered. No: the button exists for when you want to look.

steps.headline: Which themes should the change review show?
steps.today: The screenshot tool can photograph in any theme; more themes means more pictures.
steps.problem: Some breaks only show in one theme (e.g. text invisible on a dark background).

options.label: One light, one dark
pros: Catches most colour breaks.
Twice the pictures, not ten times.
cons: A break in a single community theme could slip by.

options.label: Only your theme
pros: Fewest pictures.
cons: Misses breaks other users see.

options.label: Every built-in theme
pros: Nothing slips.
cons: Many times the pictures and the wait.

steps.intro: What happens to the 1,255 existing test files.

steps.headline: The ~79% of tests that try real code and check the result stay.
steps.changed: Sorting 150 random tests found most check real outcomes of one part: a file saved, a secret kept off disk, a crash not losing data. They're fast and catch real logic mistakes.
steps.notice: Nothing for you. They keep running on every change; the new real-app check covers what they can't — the assembled app.

steps.headline: Build the new real-app checks first, or delete the wording tests first?
steps.today: The wording/style tests are annoying but harmless; the real-app check doesn't exist yet.
steps.problem: Order decides which problem gets fixed sooner.

options.label: Real checks first
pros: The thing that would have caught the phone failure exists soonest.
No stretch where coverage drops.
cons: The wording tests keep causing busywork a bit longer.

options.label: Delete wording tests first
pros: Quick win; less busywork right away.
cons: Delays the check that actually protects users.

options.label: Both at once
pros: Everything moves together.
cons: Bigger, slower to review; more chance something is missed.
